title: Are Viruses Alive?
hook: A virus is little more than genes in a protein shell — it can't eat, grow, or reproduce on its own, which is why biologists still argue whether it counts as living.
key_points: A virus is genetic material (DNA or RNA) wrapped in a protein coat.
Viruses can't reproduce alone — they must hijack a host cell's machinery.
They are far smaller than bacteria and are not made of cells.
Because they fail the usual tests for life, their living status is genuinely debated.
content_html: A virus sits right on the blurry border between life and non-life. Strip it down and it's astonishingly simple: a short string of genetic material — DNA or RNA — packed inside a protein coat, sometimes with an outer envelope. It has no cell, no metabolism, and no way to make energy. By itself, a virus is inert, more like a chemical package than a creature.
extra_html: The catch is reproduction. A virus can't copy itself; it has to get inside a living cell and commandeer that cell's machinery to manufacture new virus particles, often destroying the host in the process. Because it can't grow, respond, or reproduce independently, a virus fails several standard criteria for life — which is why many biologists describe viruses as existing "at the edge of life" rather than firmly alive. This also explains why antibiotics, which attack bacterial structures, are useless against them; fighting viruses needs vaccines or antiviral drugs instead. Britannica lays out the structure and the lifecycle.

related.title: What Are Bacteria?
related.hook: Single-celled and everywhere — in soil, oceans, and your gut — bacteria run much of the planet's chemistry, and most of them never make you sick.

related.title: What Is a Cell?
related.hook: Every living thing — from a bacterium to a blue whale — is built from cells, the smallest unit that can call itself alive.

related.title: Viruses as Age-Distorters
related.hook: Could an infection leave you biologically older? In flies, the worse a virus was, the more it sped up aging — and the effect lingered after the virus was gone.

flashcards.prompt: Why can't a virus reproduce on its own?
flashcards.back_html: It lacks the machinery to copy itself, so it must hijack a living host cell and use that cell's equipment to make more viruses.

flashcards.prompt: What is a virus basically made of?

choices.text: Genetic material wrapped in a protein coat
A complete cell with a nucleus
A cluster of bacteria stuck together

flashcards.explanation_html: A virus is just genes (DNA or RNA) inside a protein shell — it is not a cell and has no internal machinery of its own.

flashcards.prompt: Will antibiotics cure a viral infection like the flu?

choices.text: No — antibiotics target bacteria, not viruses
Yes — but only the strongest ones

flashcards.explanation_html: Viruses lack the bacterial structures antibiotics attack, so the drugs do nothing against them — antivirals or vaccines are the tools that work.
